angle: 20 beginner investing mistakes, from 3 angles: numbers, psychology, playbook
title: 20 Investing Mistakes Beginners Make in 2027

scenes.text: Hi, I'm Ryan Rover. Investing has never been easier to start. You can open an account on your phone in minutes, buy a fraction of a share with a few dollars, and trade without paying commissions. But easier to start doesn't mean easier to do well. In fact, it's never been easier to make expensive beginner mistakes. Today we're going through twenty of them, and what to do instead.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Here's the good news. Most investing mistakes aren't about picking the wrong stock. They're about waiting too long, paying too much, reacting too emotionally and skipping the basics. And every one of those can be fixed.

card.label: Beginner investing mistakes
card.sub: and what to do instead of each one

scenes.short_hook: Most beginner investors lose money for the same few reasons.

scenes.text: Think about it like learning to drive. Most crashes don't happen because someone lacked advanced racing skills. They happen because of basic mistakes, like speeding, not paying attention or panicking at the wrong moment. Investing works the same way. Avoiding the big basic mistakes matters far more than finding a clever strategy.
scenes.caption: BASICS BEAT CLEVERNESS

scenes.text: We'll go through these from three angles. First, the numbers. Mistakes that quietly cost you money through math, like waiting, fees and taxes. Second, the psychology. Mistakes our brains push us into, like panic and hype. And third, the playbook. Mistakes in how people set up and run their investments. Quick reminder, this is education, not financial advice, and all growth examples are illustrations, not promises.
scenes.caption: THREE ANGLES

scenes.text: Let's start with the numbers. And the first mistake is the most expensive one of all.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Our numbers. Growth examples use monthly compounding at a stated average yearly return, usually seven percent. Account and tax rules come from the IRS. Fund cost data comes from the Investment Company Institute, and fund performance data from S and P Dow Jones Indices. Investor warnings come from the SEC and FINRA. This is education, not financial advice.
scenes.caption: OUR NUMBERS

scenes.text: Angle one. The numbers. Seven mistakes that quietly cost beginners money, often without them ever noticing.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Mistake number one. Waiting for the right time to start.
scenes.caption: MISTAKE 1

scenes.text: Beginners often wait. For a bigger paycheck, for the market to drop, for more knowledge, for less stress. But the most important ingredient in investing is time, and every year you wait is a year of compounding you can never get back. Waiting feels safe, but it's often the most expensive choice of all.
scenes.caption: WAITING FEELS SAFE

scenes.text: Here's the math. Two hundred dollars a month at a seven percent average yearly return, invested for thirty five years, grows to roughly three hundred sixty thousand dollars. Start ten years later and invest for twenty five years, and it grows to roughly one hundred sixty two thousand. Waiting ten years cut the result by more than half.
scenes.caption: $360K VS $162K

scenes.text: Waiting for the market to dip is a special version of this mistake. Nobody can reliably predict short term moves. People who wait for a crash sometimes watch the market rise for years before it comes, and by then, the crash may still leave prices higher than when they started waiting.
scenes.caption: WAITING FOR A DIP

scenes.text: What to do instead. Start now with whatever you can, even fifty or one hundred dollars a month, and increase it over time. You'll learn more from one year of actually investing than from five years of waiting to feel ready.
scenes.caption: START NOW, START SMALL

scenes.text: Mistake number two. Ignoring fees.
scenes.caption: MISTAKE 2

scenes.text: Fees look tiny because they're shown as percentages. One percent a year sounds like nothing. But that percentage comes out of your whole balance, every year, for decades. Beginners often don't even know what they're paying.
scenes.caption: FEES HIDE IN PERCENTAGES

scenes.text: According to the Investment Company Institute, the average index equity mutual fund recently charged around five hundredths of a percent a year, while the average actively managed equity fund charged around sixty five hundredths. Over forty years of steady investing, a gap like that can cost hundreds of thousands of dollars.
scenes.caption: 0.05% VS 0.65%

scenes.text: And fund fees aren't the only ones. Some advisors charge around one percent a year on top of fund fees. Some accounts charge maintenance fees. Some products have sales charges when you buy. Fees stack, and they compound against you.
scenes.caption: FEES STACK UP

scenes.text: Here's a quick way to see fees in dollars. Multiply your balance by the expense ratio. On a fifty thousand dollar balance, a one percent fee is five hundred dollars a year. A five hundredths of a percent fee is twenty five dollars. Same market exposure in many cases, very different cost, and that difference compounds every single year.
scenes.caption: $500 VS $25 A YEAR

scenes.text: What to do instead. Find the expense ratio of every fund you own, and know exactly how any advisor is paid. Favor broad, low cost index funds, and treat every fee as something that has to justify itself.
scenes.caption: KNOW EVERY FEE

scenes.text: Mistake number three. Skipping the employer match.
scenes.caption: MISTAKE 3

scenes.text: Many employers match part of what you contribute to a workplace retirement plan. A common example is fifty cents for every dollar you contribute, up to six percent of your salary. Not contributing enough to get the full match is like turning down part of your pay.
scenes.caption: THE MATCH IS PART OF YOUR PAY
scenes.short_hook: If your job offers this and you skip it, you're turning down free money.

scenes.text: Here's what that can mean. On a sixty thousand dollar salary, contributing six percent is three thousand six hundred dollars a year, and a fifty percent match adds one thousand eight hundred. Invested for thirty years at a seven percent average yearly return, that match alone could grow to roughly one hundred eighty thousand dollars.
scenes.caption: THE MATCH COULD BE $180K

scenes.text: Some matches come with a vesting schedule, meaning you have to stay a certain number of years to keep all of the employer's money. Even so, for most people, getting the match is one of the best returns available anywhere.
scenes.caption: CHECK THE VESTING

scenes.text: What to do instead. Find your plan's match formula in your benefits information, and set your contribution at least high enough to get every dollar of it.
scenes.caption: GET THE FULL MATCH

scenes.text: Mistake number four. Investing while carrying high interest debt.
scenes.caption: MISTAKE 4

scenes.text: Investing feels more exciting than paying off debt. But credit card interest rates in the United States have averaged above twenty percent in recent years, according to Federal Reserve data. Long term stock market returns have historically been much lower than that.
scenes.caption: 20% DEBT VS MARKET RETURNS

scenes.text: So if you invest while carrying a large credit card balance, you're usually losing the race. The debt grows faster than your investments are likely to. Paying off a twenty percent card is like earning a guaranteed twenty percent return.
scenes.caption: A RACE YOU USUALLY LOSE

scenes.text: The exception is usually the employer match. Many people still contribute enough to get it while paying down debt, because the match is such a high immediate return.
scenes.caption: THE MATCH EXCEPTION

scenes.text: What to do instead. List your debts by interest rate. Attack the highest rate first while making minimum payments on the rest, then redirect those payments into investing once the expensive debt is gone.
scenes.caption: HIGHEST RATE FIRST

scenes.text: Mistake number five. Investing without an emergency fund.

card.title: No emergency fund
card.sub: forced to sell at the worst time

scenes.caption: MISTAKE 5

scenes.text: Picture this. You invest everything you have. Then the market drops, and around the same time, your car breaks down or you lose your job. Now you have to sell investments at a loss to pay bills. That's how beginners turn temporary drops into permanent losses.
scenes.caption: FORCED TO SELL LOW

scenes.text: An emergency fund is cash set aside for surprises, often three to six months of essential expenses, kept somewhere safe and easy to reach, like a high yield savings account. It's not an investment. It's insurance for your investments.
scenes.caption: INSURANCE FOR YOUR INVESTMENTS

scenes.text: It also helps you stay calm. When you know your bills are covered, market drops feel less scary. You can leave your investments alone and let them recover, instead of panicking.
scenes.caption: CASH CREATES CALM

scenes.text: What to do instead. Build at least a starter emergency fund, maybe one thousand dollars, before investing heavily, then grow it toward three to six months of essentials over time.
scenes.caption: BUILD THE CUSHION FIRST

scenes.text: Mistake number six. Expecting smooth returns.
scenes.caption: MISTAKE 6

scenes.text: Beginners often hear that the stock market has averaged around ten percent a year historically, before inflation, and expect something close to that every year. But averages hide huge swings. Individual years can be up thirty percent or down more than thirty percent.
scenes.caption: AVERAGES HIDE SWINGS

scenes.text: The S and P five hundred fell by more than a third in 2008. It dropped sharply in early 2020, then recovered quickly. In 2022 it fell by around a fifth. Long term investors have been rewarded historically, but the path has never been smooth.
scenes.caption: THE PATH IS NEVER SMOOTH

scenes.text: Here's another quirk of the math. If your investment falls thirty percent, you need a gain of about forty three percent just to get back to even. Losses and gains aren't symmetrical, which is one more reason to avoid panic selling after a drop.
scenes.caption: -30% NEEDS +43%

scenes.text: It also helps to know how often bad years happen. Historically, the S and P five hundred has had a negative calendar year roughly one year in four, give or take. That means a forty year investing life could include about ten losing years. They are not a sign that something is broken. They are the price of admission for long term growth.
scenes.query: Calendar with red and green years
scenes.caption: ROUGHLY 1 YEAR IN 4 IS DOWN

scenes.text: What to do instead. Plan for bad years. Expect them, write down how you'll respond, and only invest money in stocks that you won't need for at least five years.
scenes.caption: PLAN FOR BAD YEARS

scenes.text: Mistake number seven. Ignoring taxes.

card.title: Ignoring taxes
card.sub: the wrong account, the wrong timing

scenes.caption: MISTAKE 7

scenes.text: Taxes can take a big bite out of returns, but beginners often ignore them. One common mistake is investing in a regular taxable account while ignoring tax advantaged accounts like a four oh one k, a traditional IRA or a Roth IRA.
scenes.caption: USE TAX ADVANTAGED ACCOUNTS

scenes.text: Another is selling too quickly. In the United States, profits on investments held one year or less are generally taxed as ordinary income, while investments held longer than a year usually qualify for lower long term capital gains rates. Frequent trading can mean paying more tax.
scenes.caption: HOLD OVER A YEAR

scenes.text: Each tax advantaged account has rules, income limits and yearly contribution limits that change over time. The IRS website lists the current numbers.
scenes.caption: KNOW THE RULES

scenes.text: What to do instead. Use tax advantaged accounts first where it makes sense, hold investments for the long term, and consider talking to a tax professional if your situation is complex.
scenes.caption: TAXES ARE PART OF RETURNS

scenes.text: That's angle one. Waiting, fees, skipping the match, expensive debt, no emergency fund, expecting smooth returns and ignoring taxes. Now angle two. The psychology.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Most investing mistakes aren't caused by a lack of knowledge. They're caused by emotions. Fear, greed, excitement, envy. In this angle, we'll look at seven mistakes our brains push us into, and how to protect yourself from your own instincts.
scenes.caption: EMOTIONS DRIVE MISTAKES

scenes.text: Mistake number eight. Panic selling during a crash.
scenes.caption: MISTAKE 8

scenes.text: When markets fall, it feels like the drop will never end. The news is scary, your balance is shrinking and every instinct says get out before it gets worse. So many beginners sell, turning a temporary paper loss into a real, permanent one.
scenes.caption: THE URGE TO GET OUT
scenes.short_hook: The worst investing move happens when you're most scared.

scenes.text: The problem is that some of the market's best days have historically come close to its worst ones. Investors who sell in a panic often miss the rebound, and then buy back in later at higher prices, if they buy back at all.
scenes.caption: MISSING THE REBOUND

scenes.text: Historically, the broad U.S. market has recovered from every past crash, although some recoveries took years and there's no guarantee for the future. The investors who stayed in through those drops were usually the ones rewarded.
scenes.caption: STAYING IN HAS BEEN REWARDED

scenes.text: There's also a hidden cost to panic selling in a taxable account. If you sell investments that had gains, you may owe taxes, and if you buy back later, you start over with a new cost basis. So panic can cost you twice, once in missed recovery and once in taxes. Staying invested avoids both.
scenes.caption: PANIC CAN COST YOU TWICE

scenes.text: What to do instead. Decide now how you'll act in a crash. Write it down. When a crash comes, keep your automatic investments running and avoid making big decisions while you're scared.
scenes.caption: DECIDE BEFORE THE CRASH

scenes.text: Mistake number nine. Chasing last year's winners.
scenes.caption: MISTAKE 9

scenes.text: Beginners often look at which fund or stock went up the most last year and buy it. It feels logical. If it went up a lot, it must be good. But past performance often doesn't continue.
scenes.caption: LAST YEAR'S WINNER

scenes.text: S and P Dow Jones Indices tracks whether top performing funds stay on top. Their persistence research has found that relatively few top funds keep their top ranking over the following years. Yesterday's winner is often tomorrow's average, or worse.
scenes.caption: WINNERS RARELY REPEAT

scenes.text: Chasing performance also means buying after prices have already risen a lot, which can mean buying high. Then, when the fund cools off, many people sell low and move to the next hot thing.
scenes.caption: BUY HIGH, SELL LOW

scenes.text: Fund companies know this, which is why advertisements often highlight a fund's best recent returns. A fund family with dozens of funds will almost always have a few with great recent numbers, just by chance. Seeing a strong track record in an ad tells you very little about what that fund will do next.
scenes.caption: ADS SHOW THE WINNERS

scenes.text: What to do instead. Choose investments based on cost, diversification and your plan, not on recent returns. Broad, low cost index funds remove the need to guess who'll win next.
scenes.caption: CHOOSE BY PLAN, NOT RETURNS

scenes.text: Mistake number ten. Falling for hype.
scenes.caption: MISTAKE 10

scenes.text: Every few years, something becomes the investment everyone's talking about. A hot sector, a meme stock, a new coin. Prices soar, people brag online and beginners rush in so they don't miss out.
scenes.caption: THE NEXT BIG THING

scenes.text: Some hyped investments keep rising for a while. But many end with sharp crashes, and the people who buy in late, often beginners, tend to buy near the top. History is full of bubbles that felt like sure things at the time.
scenes.caption: BUBBLES FEEL LIKE SURE THINGS

scenes.text: The SEC and FINRA regularly warn investors about pump and dump schemes, where promoters hype an investment to push its price up, then sell their own shares to the people they convinced to buy.
scenes.caption: BEWARE PUMP AND DUMP

scenes.text: A useful test is to ask how the investment actually makes money. A company earns profits. A bond pays interest. A rental property collects rent. If the only reason something should go up is that other people will want to buy it later at a higher price, you're speculating, not investing, and you should size it that way.
scenes.caption: HOW DOES IT MAKE MONEY?

scenes.text: What to do instead. If you want to try a speculative investment, use only a small amount you can afford to lose completely, and never borrow money to do it.
scenes.caption: ONLY WHAT YOU CAN LOSE

scenes.text: Quick pause. If this list is saving you from even one of these mistakes, please subscribe to Ryan Rover Money. It's free, and it helps us keep making these. Now, mistake eleven.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Mistake number eleven. Getting overconfident after early wins.
scenes.caption: MISTAKE 11

scenes.text: Many beginners start investing during a rising market. Their first picks go up, and they conclude they're naturally good at this. So they invest more aggressively, trade more often and take bigger risks.
scenes.caption: BEGINNER'S LUCK

scenes.text: But in a rising market, almost everything goes up. Early gains often say more about the market than about skill. When the market turns, the bigger risks lead to bigger losses.
scenes.caption: A RISING TIDE LIFTS ALL BOATS

scenes.text: Research by Brad Barber and Terrance Odean found that the individual investors who traded most often earned lower returns after costs than those who traded least. Confidence led to activity, and activity often hurt returns.
scenes.caption: MORE TRADING, LOWER RETURNS

scenes.text: What to do instead. Compare your results with a simple index fund over several years, including bad ones. If you're not beating it, the index fund is the better choice.
scenes.caption: BENCHMARK YOURSELF

scenes.text: Mistake number twelve. Checking your investments too often.
scenes.caption: MISTAKE 12

scenes.text: Investing apps make it easy to check your balance dozens of times a day. But the more often you look, the more often you see losses. Over short periods, markets go down quite often, even when they rise over the long run.
scenes.caption: MORE LOOKS, MORE LOSSES

scenes.text: Economists Shlomo Benartzi and Richard Thaler called this myopic loss aversion. Because losses feel worse than gains feel good, investors who check often feel more pain and tend to make more cautious, emotional decisions, which can hurt long term returns.
scenes.caption: MYOPIC LOSS AVERSION

scenes.text: Frequent checking also creates the urge to do something. And for long term investors, doing something is often worse than doing nothing.
scenes.caption: THE URGE TO ACT

scenes.text: Think about it this way. If you owned a rental house, you wouldn't ask for a price quote every hour and panic when it came in lower than yesterday. You'd look at the rent, the condition and the long term value. Treat your index funds the same way, as long term assets you own, not as numbers on a scoreboard.
scenes.caption: THINK LIKE AN OWNER

scenes.text: What to do instead. Turn off price notifications, move the app off your home screen, and review your investments on a schedule, like once a quarter or twice a year.
scenes.caption: CHECK ON A SCHEDULE

scenes.text: Mistake number thirteen. Taking investing advice from social media.
scenes.caption: MISTAKE 13

scenes.text: Social media is full of people sharing stock tips, trading strategies and screenshots of huge gains. Some are honest. Some are paid to promote products. Some are simply lucky. And it's very hard to tell which is which.
scenes.caption: WHO'S GIVING THE ADVICE?

scenes.text: FINRA and the SEC have warned investors about financial influencers who promote investments without disclosing that they're being paid, and about scams that use fake testimonials and impersonations. If something promises guaranteed high returns with little risk, that's a major red flag.
scenes.caption: GUARANTEED RETURNS ARE A RED FLAG

scenes.text: You also only see the winners. People rarely post their losses, so social media gives a distorted picture of how investing usually goes.
scenes.caption: YOU ONLY SEE THE WINS

scenes.text: Ask yourself how the person makes money. If they earn commissions, referral fees or sponsorships from the products they recommend, their advice may not be neutral. That doesn't make them dishonest, but it does mean you should be more skeptical, and look for independent sources before acting.
scenes.caption: FOLLOW THE MONEY

scenes.text: What to do instead. Learn from sources with accountability, like books by established authors, official resources like Investor dot gov, and fee only fiduciary advisors. And check any professional's background on FINRA's BrokerCheck.
scenes.caption: CHECK THE SOURCE

scenes.text: Mistake number fourteen. Putting too much in one company, especially your employer.
scenes.caption: MISTAKE 14

scenes.text: When Enron collapsed in 2001, many employees had a large share of their retirement savings in Enron stock. They lost their jobs and much of their retirement money at the same time. It's one of the most painful lessons in investing history.
scenes.caption: THE ENRON LESSON
scenes.short_hook: Thousands of employees lost their retirement savings because of this one mistake.

scenes.text: Owning a lot of your employer's stock feels natural. You know the company, you believe in it and sometimes it's offered at a discount. But your paycheck already depends on that company. Putting your savings there too doubles your risk.
scenes.caption: DOUBLE RISK

scenes.text: The same goes for any single stock. Even great companies can stumble, and research by Hendrik Bessembinder has shown that most individual stocks have underperformed the overall market over their lifetimes.
scenes.caption: ANY SINGLE STOCK CAN FAIL

scenes.text: What to do instead. Many financial planners suggest keeping any single stock, including your employer's, to a small share of your portfolio, often ten percent or less. Spread the rest across broad, diversified funds.
scenes.caption: KEEP IT SMALL

scenes.text: That's angle two. Panic selling, chasing winners, hype, overconfidence, checking too often, social media advice and too much in one company. Now angle three. The playbook.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: The final six mistakes are about how people set up and manage their investments. These are often the easiest to fix, because they don't require changing your personality, just changing your system.
scenes.caption: SIX SYSTEM MISTAKES

scenes.text: Mistake number fifteen. Investing without a plan.
scenes.caption: MISTAKE 15

scenes.text: Many beginners buy investments randomly. A stock a friend mentioned, a fund they saw online, something that seemed popular. Without a plan, every decision is based on whatever feels right that day, and feelings change with the market.
scenes.caption: NO MAP

scenes.text: A simple plan answers a few questions. What is this money for? When will I need it? How much will I invest each month? What mix of stocks and bonds will I hold? And what will I do when the market crashes?
scenes.caption: FIVE SIMPLE QUESTIONS

scenes.text: Professional investors often use a written investment policy statement for exactly this reason. Writing it down when you're calm protects you from decisions made when you're emotional.
scenes.caption: WRITE IT WHEN CALM

scenes.text: Your plan should also include your rules for changes. For example, I'll only change my mix if my goals or timeline change, not because of the news. I'll review once a year. I'll increase contributions with every raise. Rules like these turn dozens of emotional decisions into a few calm ones.
scenes.caption: RULES FOR CHANGES

scenes.text: What to do instead. Write a one page plan this week. Keep it somewhere you'll see it, and read it before making any big investment decision.
scenes.caption: ONE PAGE PLAN

scenes.text: Mistake number sixteen. Making it too complicated.
scenes.caption: MISTAKE 16

scenes.text: Some beginners think more investments means more safety. So they buy ten or fifteen funds, a handful of stocks and accounts at several brokerages. But many of those funds often hold the same companies, so they add complexity without much real diversification.
scenes.caption: MORE ISN'T SAFER

scenes.text: Complexity makes it harder to know what you own, harder to rebalance and easier to make mistakes. It also makes it easier to lose track of accounts and fees.
scenes.caption: COMPLEXITY CAUSES MISTAKES

scenes.text: Many successful investors use just two to four broad funds. Some use a single target date fund that holds a diversified mix and adjusts it automatically over time.
scenes.caption: TWO TO FOUR FUNDS

scenes.text: What to do instead. Check the top holdings of each fund you own. If several look nearly identical, simplify. A portfolio you understand is a portfolio you can stick with.
scenes.caption: SIMPLIFY

scenes.text: Mistake number seventeen. Using margin, leverage or options as a beginner.

card.title: Using leverage and options too early

scenes.caption: MISTAKE 17
scenes.chapter: 17. Using leverage and options too early

scenes.text: Many trading apps make it easy to borrow money to invest, called trading on margin, or to trade options and leveraged funds. These tools can multiply gains, but they also multiply losses, sometimes beyond what you put in.
scenes.caption: MULTIPLIED LOSSES

scenes.text: With margin, if your investments fall far enough, your broker can demand more money or sell your holdings, often at the worst possible time. Beginners can lose much more than they expected, very quickly.
scenes.caption: MARGIN CALLS

scenes.text: Leveraged ETFs are designed for short term trading. Because they reset daily, their long term results can differ sharply from what people expect. The SEC has published investor alerts about them.
scenes.caption: LEVERAGED ETFS ARE SHORT TERM TOOLS

scenes.text: Options deserve their own warning. They can be useful tools for experienced investors, but many beginners use them as lottery tickets, buying short term contracts that often expire worthless. Without a deep understanding of how options are priced, it's very easy to lose your entire stake in a matter of days.
scenes.caption: OPTIONS AS LOTTERY TICKETS

scenes.text: What to do instead. Stick with simple, unleveraged investments until you have years of experience, and understand exactly how any complex product works before using it.
scenes.caption: KEEP IT SIMPLE

scenes.text: Mistake number eighteen. Never rebalancing.
scenes.caption: MISTAKE 18

scenes.text: Say you start with seventy percent stocks and thirty percent bonds. After a few strong years for stocks, you might drift to eighty five percent stocks without noticing. Your portfolio is now riskier than you planned.
scenes.caption: YOUR RISK DRIFTS

scenes.text: Rebalancing means bringing your mix back to your target. You trim what grew and add to what lagged. It forces you to sell a bit high and buy a bit low, the opposite of what emotions usually push you to do.
scenes.caption: SELL HIGH, BUY LOW

scenes.text: Target date funds rebalance automatically. If you hold separate funds, a yearly check is plenty for most people.
scenes.caption: ONCE A YEAR

scenes.text: What to do instead. Pick a date each year to check your mix. If it has drifted more than about five percentage points, rebalance, ideally using new contributions to avoid selling.
scenes.caption: PICK A DATE

scenes.text: Mistake number nineteen. Forgetting old accounts and beneficiaries.
scenes.caption: MISTAKE 19

scenes.text: People change jobs many times over a career, and old retirement accounts get left behind. Some studies estimate there are millions of forgotten four oh one k accounts in the United States, holding large amounts of money. Old accounts can carry higher fees and are easy to lose track of.
scenes.caption: FORGOTTEN ACCOUNTS

scenes.text: Another overlooked detail is beneficiaries. Retirement accounts usually pass to whoever is named as beneficiary on the account, which can override what a will says. An outdated beneficiary can send money to the wrong person.
scenes.caption: UPDATE BENEFICIARIES

scenes.text: Neither of these is exciting, which is exactly why they get ignored. But a single afternoon of paperwork can protect years of savings.
scenes.caption: BORING BUT IMPORTANT

scenes.text: If you think you might have lost track of an old account, there are ways to look. Contact former employers' benefits departments, check old statements, and search the Department of Labor's retirement savings lost and found database, created under recent federal legislation to help people find old plans.
scenes.caption: FIND LOST ACCOUNTS

scenes.text: What to do instead. List every account you've ever had. Consider rolling old workplace plans into your current plan or an IRA, and check the beneficiaries on each one.
scenes.caption: LIST EVERY ACCOUNT

scenes.text: Mistake number twenty. Never increasing what you invest.
scenes.caption: MISTAKE 20

scenes.text: Many beginners start investing a small amount, which is great, and then never change it. Ten years later, they earn much more, but they're still investing the same amount as when they started.
scenes.caption: STUCK AT THE START

scenes.text: Economists Richard Thaler and Shlomo Benartzi designed Save More Tomorrow, where employees agreed in advance to increase their savings rate with each raise. Participants in their study ended up saving far more than before.
scenes.caption: SAVE MORE TOMORROW

scenes.text: Increasing contributions over time can matter as much as the return you earn. Your investing should grow as your income grows.
scenes.caption: GROW WITH YOUR INCOME

scenes.text: What to do instead. Turn on automatic increases in your retirement plan if it offers them, or set a yearly reminder to raise your contributions by one percent of your income.
scenes.caption: ONE PERCENT MORE EACH YEAR

scenes.text: Why are these mistakes so common now? Part of the reason is that investing apps have made trading feel like a game. Colorful animations, constant notifications and one tap trades make it easy to act on impulse. Regulators have raised concerns about these game like features and how they can encourage frequent trading.
scenes.caption: INVESTING FEELS LIKE A GAME
scenes.chapter: Why these mistakes are easier than ever

scenes.text: Another reason is the flood of information. Videos, posts, chat groups and online tools all offer opinions, predictions and tips. More information doesn't automatically mean better decisions. Often it means more noise, more temptation and more confusion.
scenes.caption: MORE NOISE THAN EVER

scenes.text: And scammers have new tools too. Fake investment platforms, impersonations of well known investors and too good to be true offers are common. The basic rules still protect you. Never send money to someone you only know online, verify every platform and professional, and walk away from guaranteed returns.
scenes.caption: SCAMS ARE EVOLVING

scenes.text: Let's turn all twenty mistakes into a simple checklist. If you can tick these boxes, you're ahead of most beginners.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Box one. I have a starter emergency fund, and I'm building toward three to six months of essential expenses. Box two. I have no credit card debt, or I have a clear plan to pay it off, highest rate first. These two boxes protect everything else you build, because they stop a single bad month from forcing you to sell or borrow at the worst time.
scenes.query: Checklist with first two boxes ticked
scenes.caption: BOXES 1 AND 2: PROTECTION

scenes.text: Box three. I contribute at least enough to get my full employer match. Box four. I use tax advantaged accounts, like a four oh one k or an IRA, before a regular taxable account where that makes sense. These two boxes are the closest thing investing has to free money, and skipping them is one of the most common and expensive beginner mistakes.
scenes.caption: BOXES 3 AND 4: FREE MONEY

scenes.text: Box five. My money is in broad, low cost funds, and I know the expense ratio of every one. Box six. I own two to four funds, or a single target date fund, and I understand what each one holds. Simple and cheap is not a compromise. For most people, it's the strategy that works best over decades.
scenes.caption: BOXES 5 AND 6: SIMPLE AND CHEAP

scenes.text: Box seven. My contributions are automatic, and they increase every year. Box eight. I have a one page written plan, including what I'll do in a crash. Box nine. I review my portfolio once or twice a year and rebalance if needed. Box ten. My beneficiaries are up to date, and I know where every account is.
scenes.caption: BOXES 7 TO 10: THE SYSTEM

scenes.text: Ten boxes. None of them require predicting the market, picking stocks or watching the news. That's the secret most beginners miss. Successful investing is mostly about building a good system and then leaving it alone long enough to work.
scenes.caption: BUILD THE SYSTEM, THEN LEAVE IT

scenes.text: In your twenties, the biggest mistakes are usually waiting, chasing hype and carrying expensive debt. Your greatest asset is time, so the best move is to start small, automate and avoid gambling with money you'll need. Even modest amounts invested now have decades to compound.
scenes.caption: IN YOUR 20s

scenes.text: In your thirties and forties, the big risks shift. Lifestyle creep, skipping increases as income rises, too much employer stock and forgotten old accounts from job changes. This is the stage to raise contributions, consolidate accounts and protect your family with insurance and updated beneficiaries.
scenes.caption: IN YOUR 30s AND 40s

scenes.text: In your fifties and beyond, the biggest mistakes are often taking too much risk too close to needing the money, or panicking and selling everything after a drop. A thoughtful mix of stocks, bonds and cash, plus catch up contributions after fifty, can help. Check current limits with the IRS.
scenes.caption: IN YOUR 50s AND BEYOND

scenes.text: Imagine two beginners who both start investing three hundred dollars a month. The first one downloads a trading app, buys whatever is trending, checks constantly, sells during the first big drop and jumps back in after prices recover. After a few years, they've paid more in taxes, missed the rebound and feel that investing doesn't work.
scenes.caption: BEGINNER ONE
scenes.short_hook: Two beginners started investing the same year. Only one made money.

scenes.text: The second one opens a retirement account, gets the full employer match, picks one low cost target date fund, automates contributions and checks twice a year. During the same drop, they keep investing, buying shares at lower prices. Their plan is boring, and it's working.
scenes.caption: BEGINNER TWO

scenes.text: Same income. Same market. Same starting amount. The difference wasn't intelligence or luck. It was avoiding a handful of basic mistakes. That's the real secret of beginner investing.
scenes.caption: THE DIFFERENCE WAS MISTAKES

scenes.text: Question one. What's the single biggest mistake? For most people, it's not starting, or starting late. Time in the market is the ingredient you can't buy back. Many other mistakes can be fixed later. Lost years can't.
scenes.caption: THE BIGGEST MISTAKE

scenes.text: Question two. I've already made some of these mistakes. Is it too late? Not at all. Almost every investor has made some of them. The best time to fix them is now. Simplify, cut fees, automate, and keep going.
scenes.caption: IS IT TOO LATE?

scenes.text: Question three. Do I need a financial advisor? Not necessarily. Many people do well with a simple, low cost plan on their own. If you want help, look for a fee only fiduciary, who's required to act in your best interest, and understand exactly what you're paying.
scenes.caption: DO I NEED AN ADVISOR?

scenes.text: Question four. Should I invest a lump sum all at once, or spread it out? Historically, investing a lump sum right away has often come out ahead, because markets have risen more often than they've fallen. But spreading it over several months can feel easier emotionally. Either is far better than leaving money uninvested for years while you decide.
scenes.caption: LUMP SUM OR SPREAD IT?

scenes.text: Question five. How much should I have in stocks versus bonds? It depends on your timeline and how well you handle drops. A common starting point is to hold more stocks when your goal is decades away and gradually add bonds as it gets closer. Target date funds do this for you automatically.
scenes.caption: STOCKS OR BONDS?

scenes.text: Question six. Is it okay to invest if I don't understand everything yet? Yes. You don't need to understand every detail to start with a simple, diversified, low cost fund. You can keep learning while your money works. Just avoid anything complex you can't explain in a sentence or two.
scenes.caption: DO I NEED TO KNOW EVERYTHING?

scenes.text: Quick recap. Angle one, the numbers. Waiting, fees, skipping the match, expensive debt, no emergency fund, expecting smooth returns and ignoring taxes.
scenes.caption: THE NUMBERS: 1 TO 7

scenes.text: Angle two, the psychology. Panic selling, chasing winners, hype, overconfidence, checking too often, social media advice and too much in one company.
scenes.caption: THE PSYCHOLOGY: 8 TO 14

scenes.text: Angle three, the playbook. No plan, too much complexity, leverage too early, never rebalancing, forgotten accounts and never increasing contributions.
scenes.caption: THE PLAYBOOK: 15 TO 20

scenes.text: You don't need to be brilliant to invest well. You just need to avoid the big mistakes, keep it simple and give it time. If you want my full step by step plan, it's in my playbook, linked in the description. Tell me in the comments, which of these mistakes have you made? I'm Ryan Rover. See you in the next one.
scenes.caption: RYAN
